<reason>PRO (B) won by narrowing the debate to a single decisive question: is the sex field already a revisable administrative descriptor? CON's opening depended on the marker being "objective, stable, externally checkable," but under pressure (A4.1) CON conceded that existing marker changes already cut the anchor and admitted opposing those changes too—placing CON's position outside the actual status quo the motion operates in. B pressed this in B4.7 and B5.1 effectively. B also neutralized CON's function arguments (doctors examine unconscious patients regardless; intake officers already override the letter; verification runs on face and number) and answered the outing argument with the option-not-mandate point. CON's Q1/Q2 were fair pressure, but B answered them directly (same attestation standard, no fraud motive for a stigmatizing marker, enabling statutes name defaults). CON's response to B's request for a real-world failure—"diffused friction" hidden by low uptake—was honest but let B frame the clash as evidence versus hypotheticals. CON stayed coherent and had a real point that the letter is meant to guide until overridden (A4.3), but never recovered the anchor premise. B's two clipped turns are an execution cost but did not remove key material.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's A1 answer plus B4.7/B5.1: pinning CON's admission that markers already change and that CON opposes those changes, showing CON's "objective marker" defends a system no state prints, while the unconscious-patient example already fails under current law.</best_rebuttal>
